items.title: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 3,697 new readers. The Jensen Huang saga already felt like a movie. On Monday, the scandal that had rocked the tech world for weeks hit its climax — the return.

Jensen is back in the captain's seat at Nvidia, leather jacket and all, after President Donald Trump personally lobbied the board and its members voted unanimously to reinstate him. With it came $1T in market value, celebrations from the tech world, and fresh outrage on Capitol Hill.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia

  • Meta's AI chief: superintelligence is ‘arriving’

  • Go beyond the browser with the Claude desktop app

  • OpenAI pays locals to bring AI to small businesses

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

JENSEN HUANG & NVIDIA

🔁 Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia

Image source: @aburducky on X

The Rundown: Nvidia's board just reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO only 11 days after he resigned over affairs with a direct report and a woman U.S. officials linked to Chinese intelligence, with President Trump saying he personally pushed for the return.

The details:

  • The unanimous vote came six days after chair Harvey Jones ruled out rehiring Huang, with the board saying “senior levels” of the U.S. government weighed in.

  • Huang said he takes the job back “with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” thanking interim CEO Colette Kress, who stays on as CFO.

  • Trump told CNBC he'd been “speaking to the board directly and indirectly,” and posted that the government sees no reason to view Huang's return as a risk.

  • Nvidia shares jumped over 30% after the open and added over $1T in market value during trading, the single largest daily gain in the history of the stock market.

  • Huang still faces a House hearing in December, with Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries calling the move “indefensible, irresponsible, and incomprehensible.”

Why it matters: Absolute cinema. The Jensen saga has hit every peak and valley in under a month: Nvidia's initial denial, a resignation, a board that insisted he wasn't coming back, and now a presidential intervention and return. But with lawmakers already pushing back and a House hearing set for Dec. 1, his case is far from closed.

TOGETHER WITH STACK AI

🚀 Enterprise AI, deployed with experts

The Rundown: With the detail of Palantir and the scale of Salesforce, StackAI is the enterprise AI agent platform with a dedicated team of AI experts who handle integration, security, and on-prem deployment, and get your agents into production on your data.

With StackAI, you get:

  • A no-code platform for complex use cases

  • An AI strategist who tracks your ROI

  • An engineer who builds your custom workflows

Meet your AI deployment team.

META

🚨 Meta's AI chief: superintelligence is ‘arriving’

Image source: @alexandr_wang on X

The Rundown: Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang just posted an essay on X declaring that “Superintelligence is arriving,” urging the industry to take “meaningfully different actions” from the “default path” it's on towards superintelligent AI.

The details:

  • Wang cited Claude's help proving the Riemann hypothesis, saying AI could speed up “nearly every field” beyond what “humans can understand or monitor.”

  • Wang, who was raised in Los Alamos, said many physicists would call the atomic bomb “a homework problem compared to the Riemann Hypothesis.”

  • He also said intelligence no longer holds AI back, predicting models will soon handle all of AI research and be “superhuman at improving themselves.”

  • He called it “lazy thinking” when parts of the industry treat superintelligence as inevitable, and said society should not accept a “handover” to AI.

Why it matters: This is quite the departure from the usually lighthearted, meme-happy Wang — and from his boss, Mark Zuckerberg, who has typically pushed back on slowdown calls and AI “doom” talk. As head of one of AI's biggest labs, Wang can also do more than post about it, so we’ll have to wait and see if Meta's actions actually follow.

AI TRAINING

🖥️ Go beyond the browser with the Claude desktop app

The Rundown: In this guide, you will weigh Claude in the browser against the Claude desktop app, then install the app and set it up.

Step-by-step:

  1. Decide where you’ll use Claude. You can stay in the browser on a computer you share or borrow, and install the app on the one you use most days

  2. Go to claude.com/download, find your system under Desktop, and click Download

  3. On a Mac, open Claude.dmg and drag Claude into the Applications folder. On Windows, open the file you downloaded, and the installer does the rest

  4. Open Claude and sign in with the account you use at claude.ai. Your chats and projects are already there

  5. On Mac, enable ‘Turn on shortcut’ when Claude offers quick entry, and click Continue. Then, you can double-tap the Option key in any app to ask Claude

Pro tip: Keep the browser for computers you share or borrow, and the app for your own. It’s the same account in both, so your chats never get split between them.

Same open-weights model, same 1M-token context window, served at a fraction of the usual cost. Ready to use in agent workflows and automation tools such as n8n.

With CompactifAI API, developers can:

  • Run GLM 5.3 for 70% less than Z.ai’s own API

  • Switch current provider by changing only the base URL, no new SDK needed

OPENAI

🏪 OpenAI pays locals to bring AI to small businesses

Image source: OpenAI

The Rundown: OpenAI just debuted OpenWorks, a pilot that pays tech-savvy locals to sit down with small business owners in 20 U.S. cities and help them put AI to work on a task or problem the owner picks at no cost.

The details:

  • Partners set aside days each month for hands-on work with owners and teach one community AI class a month, with OpenAI paying stipends of up to $8,000 monthly.

  • The pilot leans away from tech hubs, with 15 of 20 cities in the Midwest or South, aimed at independent restaurants, shops, factories, and service businesses.

  • Participating businesses get 3 free months of ChatGPT Business, while software, venture-backed, and private equity-owned firms are excluded from applying.

Why it matters: Time and money are two of the biggest hurdles for small business owners, and OpenWorks takes a swing at both — with a local expert who builds alongside them, plus three months of ChatGPT. For tech-savvy locals, it's also a paid on-ramp into AI consulting, and for OAI, a pipeline of new potential Business customers.

It's built for anyone who tracks marketing across several platforms and wants the reporting done automatically.

I created a sheet in my Google Drive to serve as my marketing tracker. I linked Metricool to track my social accounts. My email program isn't linked yet, so for now I take screenshots of my weekly email reports and add them to the chat.

items.title: Claude helps solve math's biggest open problem
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 8,176 new readers. Few fields have changed more under AI this past year than math. Now, a single Anthropic mathematician and Claude may have solved a problem even the top minds thought was years, if not decades, away.

Levent Alpöge says they just proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old prime-number puzzle that carries a $1M Millennium Prize and has long been seen as math's most famous open problem. As with AI's other big math wins, not everyone is thrilled.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Claude helps solve math's biggest open problem

  • The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

  • Test Gemini 4 Neon on finding billing errors

  • OpenAI opens its private AI scorecard to rivals

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

ANTHROPIC, AI, & MATHEMATICS

🧮 Claude helps solve math's biggest open problem

Image source: Claude / The Rundown

The Rundown: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge used Claude to crack the Riemann hypothesis, the 167-year-old question often ranked as math's biggest unsolved problem, after ~6 weeks of work, and checkers say it holds up, even as no human fully gets it yet.

The details:

  • First posed in 1859, the problem asks whether prime numbers follow a predictable pattern, and the Clay Institute put a $1M “Millennium” prize on solving it in 2000.

  • Alpöge shared the proof only as 17M lines of machine-checkable math, writing that Claude “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

  • The groups behind Lean, the computer language used for verification, certified it on Saturday, saying they have “full confidence” that Alpöge’s proof is correct.

  • The Association for Human Mathematics criticized the proof as “little more than publicity” for AI labs, saying no human could reasonably understand it.

  • A rival proof from Alessandro Masullo surfaced hours later, reportedly made without AI over nearly 12 years, though others quickly flagged problems in it.

Why it matters: The Riemann hypothesis was a problem top mathematicians expected to take decades of new theory to solve, and Alpöge and Claude just blew past those estimates. This proof may not change daily life, but once that speed of progress spreads to fields like biology and drug design, the practical payoff will really start to show up.

TOGETHER WITH GRANOLA

📞 Walk into every call already prepared

The Rundown: You’re two minutes out from a call and can’t remember what you discussed last time. Granola Briefs does the prep for you overnight, so you join with a few lines of context already waiting.

With Briefs, you can:

  • See who you’re meeting and what you discussed last time

  • Catch up on recent company news before you join the call

  • Trace every point back to its source when you need to dig deeper

Try Granola free. Get 1 month off any paid plan with code THERUNDOWN.

THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE

💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.

Kenny, Head of Sales: After a good discovery call, my proposal used to take so long that the buyer's urgency faded and the details got fuzzy. This workflow fixes that. I record the call using Granola, have Claude pull out the buyer's own ask, and draft the proposal from that instead of from a rate card.

Proposals built from the buyer's own words close faster than generic decks, and offering a smaller “yes” option turns “too expensive” into “let's test it.”

Result: a proposal drafted in about 10 minutes, sent while the buyer is still engaged, with the deal history logged in the CRM.

Shubham, Editor: My investments sit across several platforms, so I use Claude to bring them into one unified dashboard. Instead of logging in to each app, I can see every mutual fund and stock I hold in one place, along with what goes into each one every month and how often.

Live holdings and company fundamentals come in through MCP connectors, so the numbers match my broker, and holdings from my other platforms appear in the same view. Claude fetches a short summary of each position and updates it daily. It sets up reminders for each SIP date, the 10% step-up every April, other amount changes, and when tax is payable.

The result is one accurate view with no logging in to each app and no spreadsheet to update by hand. Claude does the fetching, organizing, and reminding, and I make the decisions.

AI TRAINING

🧠 Test Gemini 4 Neon on finding billing errors

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll put Google’s new Gemini 4 Neon to work on an everyday job: reading a year of electricity bills against your bank’s payment history to find why the bill jumped and what was billed wrong, then drafting the dispute email.

Step-by-step:

  1. Download a year of electricity bills as PDFs and your bank’s payment history as a CSV. Delete every bank row that isn’t a payment to the utility

  2. Start a temporary chat in the Gemini app, choose Deeper analysis (4 Neon) from the model menu, and set Thinking level to High

  3. Attach both files and ask for a month-by-month table of usage, rate, and total, plus which month jumped and why

  4. Ask where each problem appears in the files: the PDF page and line, or the bank row. Check two or three of those spots yourself before you rely on them

  5. Ask for a short dispute email with every date and amount. Check it against the files, then send it to the utility

Pro tip: Ask for the evidence before you act on an answer. A model that names the page, line, or row is easy to check, and only takes a minute.

PRESENTED BY VANTA

🔎 Spot your AI governance gaps

The Rundown: Vanta’s AI governance assessment is a free, 10-minute benchmark built by Vanta’s security, compliance, and AI governance experts. With AI agents already outnumbering employees 79 to 1, see where your program stands across five domains and what to fix first.

With the assessment, you will:

  • Get your AI governance maturity score

  • Tackle unapproved tools and unclear ownership

  • Prepare for a formal readiness review

Take the assessment.

AI RESEARCH

📋 OpenAI opens its private AI scorecard to rivals

Image source: OpenAI

The Rundown: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki just published the internal scores the company uses to track the raw intelligence of its AI since GPT-3.5, asking rival labs to agree on shared limits they'd hold until tools for monitoring AI catch up.

The details:

  • The metric, log-perplexity, measures how well an AI predicts the next token; lower scores indicate better predictions, and Pachocki says it tracks with AI's big jumps.

  • Pachocki tied OpenAI's biggest new skills in cybersecurity and math to scores below 0.8, down from about 0.99 for the model behind the original ChatGPT.

  • OAI also revealed an unreleased internal model at ~0.73, with Pachocki saying they should “expect further transformative capabilities” in the 0.68–0.7 range.

  • Sam Altman called the post “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while,” saying agreeing on common limits “would be very wise.”

Why it matters: This post packs in three reveals: another call for industry-wide “common limits” on progress, a first look at where OpenAI's next internal model stands, and a marker for where the next big jump in capabilities should land. Similar to METR's report on Anthropic, the data is showing that acceleration curves aren't slowing down.

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Dave built a school-email digest that fills the family calendar

Today’s workflow comes from reader Dave Kay:

“With three kids in school, I get dozens of emails every week: homework and assignment messages from teachers, updates from sports faculty, general notices from head teachers, and digests from the school's content platforms.

I asked ChatGPT to read my emails every day. Each morning it emails me a daily summary. It creates events in my Google Calendar. On Sunday, it emails me a week-ahead summary.

The result is that a quick look at one email gives me the entire week ahead, outstanding actions, and assignment due dates. I use AI for most things, but this is my killer life hack.”

items.title: Anthropic pulls off the biggest IPO ever
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 6,136 new readers. Frontier AI is now public. Anthropic just listed on the Nasdaq in the largest-ever IPO, topping SpaceX’s record from just five months ago.

The debut minted thousands of millionaires overnight and came with a promise from CEO Dario Amodei that safety, not business or political pressure, will set the pace of its models and way forward.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Anthropic raises $81B in the largest IPO ever

  • Rowan’s Corner: 4 things that stuck with me from DealBook

  • Use AI to find a job and prepare to get hired

  • OpenAI’s agents now handle half its long research tasks

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

ANTHROPIC

🤑 Anthropic raises $81B in the largest IPO ever

Image source: Nasdaq / YouTube

The Rundown: Anthropic just started trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT after raising $81.3B in the largest IPO on record, with shares closing their first day up 17% at $97.17 and valuing the company behind the Claude AI assistant at well over $1T.

The details:

  • Demand was so strong that Anthropic priced shares at $83, above its target range, and the stock opened at $111.50, briefly valuing the company near $2T.

  • 96% of Anthropic’s 5K+ employees are now millionaires on paper, with each co-founder worth ~$20B; they’ve pledged 80% of their stock to philanthropic causes.

  • At the IPO price, Amazon’s and Google’s early stakes hit $161B and $147B, and Sound Ventures, co-founded by Ashton Kutcher, turned a $435M bet into ~$7B.

  • Before the opening bell, Amodei said AI could speed up cures for disease but pledged to pace development until its models are safe, saying Anthropic “will not bend to either business nor political pressure.”

Why it matters: Two months ago, Sam Altman ruled out an OpenAI IPO this year, calling it an “ill-advised moment” given safety concerns. Anthropic went ahead, and the lab built on safety will now face Wall Street’s scrutiny. Every earnings call will be a test of both the AI boom and Anthropic’s pledge to slow down if safety demands it.

TOGETHER WITH GLEAN

📊 Turn company data into decision-ready answers

The Rundown: AI answers are only useful when they’re grounded in trusted data and enterprise context. This eBook shows how Glean brings context to the warehouse and business intelligence tools you already use, helping teams scale self-service analytics without rebuilding their infrastructure.

  • Learn how to scale secure, self-service analytics across your business

Download the eBook.

ROWAN’S CORNER

🗽 4 things that stuck with me from DealBook

Rowan’s POV at DealBook

Rowan: I spent Wednesday at the NYT DealBook Summit, in a room that was a good mix of tech reporters, top AI execs, and Wall Street heavyweights.

Four things stuck with me:

  1. When Christine Lagarde was asked if we’re in an AI bubble, the room laughed nervously. I don’t think we are, at least not the dot-com kind. Back then, companies built capacity nobody was using yet… today, the labs can’t build compute fast enough to keep up with demand. Still, a room full of top execs laughing nervously is hard to ignore.

  2. Almost every speaker talked about Jensen leaving Nvidia. Musk compared it to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” It’s a reminder that even at trillion-dollar scale, the AI industry still runs on a handful of people.

  3. I’ve never heard Sam Altman push as hard for humans to stay in control. He called gradually handing decisions over to AI “a terrible idea” and said he doesn’t want to end up as AI’s Labrador, or his kids either. A clear shot at Elon Musk, who has said humans could end up “like a pet Labrador” to AI.

  4. Greg Brockman said the biggest differentiator between the labs will be who owns the compute. To me, that means the AI race is becoming less about who has the smartest researchers and more about who has the most chips and power.

AI TRAINING

💼 Use AI to find a job and prepare to get hired 

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use AI to find real job openings, compare them with your experience, tailor your resume, and practice for an interview. One fictional applicant carries through the full process, so you can follow along before using your own details.

Step-by-step:

  1. Choose one target job title, two related titles, and your limits for location, work setup, salary, and experience

  2. Ask ChatGPT to find five current openings. Check each role on the employer’s own careers page before adding it to your list

  3. Compare one verified job description with a redacted copy of your resume. Ask AI to show strong matches, partial matches, and missing requirements

  4. Tailor the resume and write a short cover letter using only facts you can support. Review every new claim before saving or applying

  5. Practice eight interview questions, one at a time, then add the application and next follow-up date to your tracker

Pro tip: Ask AI to show the evidence behind every resume change. A keyword is useful only when it describes work you’ve actually done.

Visit The Rundown University to get the full guide, practice resources, and more.

PRESENTED BY MEMOKET

♟️ Connect the dots. Know your next move.

The Rundown: Memoket connects business conversations to help professionals track progress, spot changes, and plan their next steps. Its Gem wearable captures those conversations with one press. Get Gem for $159 this Black Friday and save $40.

With Memoket, you can:

  • Connect client discussions and project updates to understand the full context

  • Compare conversations to spot changing needs and conflicting commitments

  • Ask for next steps grounded in past discussions, with sources to check

Get 20% off Gem.

OPENAI

🤖 OpenAI’s agents now handle half its long research tasks

Image source: OpenAI

The Rundown: OpenAI just released new data on how AI agents are speeding up its own research, finding they now complete nearly half of tasks on their own that would take a human researcher two to four hours, up from about a quarter in March.

The details:

  • Agent use is exploding, with the median OpenAI researcher running ~$2.4K of AI agent work a day, and saying they’d hypothetically give up 40% of their team headcount to keep access.

  • Each researcher now effectively runs nearly six full days of AI agent work every day, up 11x since May, with two-thirds running four or more agents at once.

  • Researchers said agents still lack taste and turn out “AI slop,” but one admitted having “no confidence” that their edge in ideas will last for long.

  • Human researchers drove every key idea behind GPT-6 Astra, but for GPT-6.2 Astra, they said Codex helped generate key insights.

Why it matters: AI that builds better AI could make progress speed up dramatically. Two leading labs say it’s already starting, with Claude leading 26% of Anthropic’s research and OpenAI’s agents handling nearly half of mid-length tasks. Humans still call the shots, but a sudden leap could come, like the breakthroughs AI recently made in math.

I store my health data as Markdown files on my laptop, including blood reports, glucose and blood pressure readings, exercise one-rep max measurements, and family health history. Every month, I export my wearable data and add it to the system. I also log meals, supplements, and sleep, and keep my strength, endurance, and longevity goals in separate files. A Focus Now doc lists what I need to prioritize each day, deferring everything else.

I use Obsidian to browse and edit these files, then open an AI app from my terminal with this context. The AI acts as my coach, providing personalized guidance based on my health data, goals, and family history. As I add advanced blood tests and scans, I plan to build a dashboard with calculated metrics such as biological age and pace of aging.”

items.title: Google’s shipping spree continues with Neon
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 12,783 new readers. Google spent most of 2026 being mocked for moving slowly. But something changed this fall, and it’s now shipping faster than ever. Maybe the key is, as Demis Hassabis put it, “alchemy at its finest.”

The company’s new Neon model is the latest step up both the periodic table and the leaderboard, carrying a mid-tier label but with scores nearing the industry’s best. With one researcher hinting at self-improving AI behind the pace, Google suddenly feels very, very back.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Google’s shipping spree continues with Neon

  • Nate’s Notebook: Ask your AI for more

  • Use AI to rewrite your LinkedIn profile

  • Pika turns AI video into a live film set

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

GOOGLE

🧪 Google’s shipping spree continues with Neon

Image source: Google

The Rundown: Google just released Gemini 4 Neon, a faster sibling to its top-end Carbon that leads Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Sol on most of Google’s tests — marking the company’s fourth Gemini 4 model in under two months.

The details:

  • Despite its mid-tier status, Neon edges Google’s top-end Carbon on Artificial Analysis’ leaderboard at 61, trailing only Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra.

  • Google’s testing has Neon beating Opus 5.5 and 6.2 Sol on 16 of 19 benchmarks, with its widest leads in long-document work, office automation, and cyber tasks.

  • Neon is now live for Google’s Pro and Ultra tier users, and its API costs $3/$15 per million input/output tokens, a quarter below Opus 5.5 and full-price Carbon.

  • The night before launch, Google’s Minkai Xu posted “many people are surprised by how fast RSI moves,” hinting self-improving AI may be behind Google’s pace.

Why it matters: For most of 2026, Google had every advantage (chips, cash, users) yet was painfully slow to ship frontier options people wanted. Whether it’s recursive self-improvement (RSI) or something else, a switch has flipped internally, and Google’s run through the periodic table (Argon, Carbon, Hydrogen, Neon) is showing up in a big way.

Secure your spot.

NATE’S NOTEBOOK

🚰 Nate’s Notebook: Ask your AI for more

The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.

Nate: Our well pump died at the cabin. The nearest hardware store is 35 minutes away, so one wrong part costs me the afternoon.

I was on the store’s clunky website, sure this one would stump Claude. I opened the Chrome extension anyway and typed: “Here’s our broken setup. I need water coming out of this faucet, and you can only use parts in stock at this one store.”

Then I watched it work, page by page. It would pick a pipe, find out it wasn’t in stock, back up, and try another route. It was wandering the aisles for me until it landed on 20 parts from different departments that were all on the shelf.

I thought that was the whole win. Then I caught myself getting ready to drive over and find all 20 myself. Years of confusing websites have trained me to pick the hassle I know. So I let Claude fill the cart, too. It told me when it was time to enter my credit card, and the whole order was waiting when I got there.

If you won’t hand a coworker the tedious stuff because it feels rude, this one is for you. I’m that person too, and I brought the same hesitation to AI. I think that feeling holds people back more than their tech skills do.

Back at the cabin, I almost let it stop me again. My first ask for assembly instructions was fine. Then I pushed for something more ambitious: a step-by-step slide deck. Here are both versions with the prompts I used.

Try it this week. Install the Claude or ChatGPT browser extension and point it at the site you dread: your health insurance portal, or that old internal tool at work that’s never getting an API.

Ask for more.

AI TRAINING

💼 Use AI to rewrite your LinkedIn profile

The Rundown: ChatGPT can rewrite your LinkedIn profile for the job you’re moving into, but left to itself, it rounds your story up. In this guide, you’ll have it ask about your real results, write a headline, About section, experience, and skills, then check every claim.

Step-by-step:

  1. Copy your LinkedIn headline, About section, one role, and your skills into a note as text, along with two or three job posts you’d apply for

  2. In ChatGPT, click the Temporary chat at the top right, pick Unpersonalized, and paste a prompt that asks for up to 5 questions first, all at once, and says “Don’t invent numbers, tools, titles, or results,” with your profile and the posts under it

  3. Answer every question, and say what you haven’t done yet. Then, ask for three headlines under 220 characters and an About section under 2,600 characters

  4. Next, ask for five experience bullets that start with a verb and up to 10 skills your experience shows

  5. Ask ChatGPT to check everything it wrote, in a table, and flag anything you didn’t say. Use the corrected versions, and copy them out before you leave the chat

Pro tip: Before you paste anything into LinkedIn, turn off Share profile updates (Me, then Settings & Privacy, then Visibility) so your network isn’t told about each change.

See what’s actually happening in your org.

AI VIDEO

🎬 Pika turns AI video into a live film set

Image source: Pika

The Rundown: AI video startup Pika just previewed Enact, an experimental tool that works like a live film set, letting users drag actors around, give them spoken notes, and move the camera while the scene keeps playing.

The details:

  • Users can set the stage by grabbing a person or object and moving it mid-scene, with the AI adjusting how it stands and where its shadow falls in the new spot.

  • Each actor is a separate AI agent with its own personality that responds to both audio and text direction and can keep track of feedback from earlier takes.

  • Once rolling, the camera is controllable throughout the live action, letting users make visual choices just like a director would on set.

  • Pika said its team was “startled by how much more real and visceral it feels” to make video this way, though Enact isn’t available to consumers yet.

Why it matters: A large portion of the world still thinks of AI video as “slop,” but the ramp-up in quality combined with control, speed, and cost-effective models has opened a new outlet for creatives. With real-time video now seeing similar gains, creating an AI video could soon look a lot like what directors are already doing in the real world.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ A reader built a ChatGPT adviser to research contacts

Today’s workflow comes from an Anonymous Rundown Reader:

“I often reach out to people I know very little about, whether it's an important email, a text, a potential collaborator, a volunteer request, or prep for a meeting. Researching someone used to take more time than most of these interactions seemed to justify.

Now I use ChatGPT to look into a person's public background, find real common ground, and plan how I'll communicate. The goal isn't to show off what I know about them. It's to communicate more intelligently and naturally.

I start with a prompt that begins: ‘Act as my personal research, communication, and rapport-building adviser.’ The full prompt also tells the AI to verify identity and important findings, separate facts from interpretation, and avoid inventing a background or assuming someone with a similar name is the right person.

What I get is a better-informed message, fewer misunderstandings, and a clear record I can return to when the relationship continues.”
